text: You could do this the long way.
Work out 2 cubed equals 8 and 2 squared equals 4, multiply them to get 32, then hunt for the exponent that makes 32.
That works here. But for 2¹⁰ times 2¹⁵ you would be counting all day.
When you multiply two numbers with the same base, keep the base and add the exponents.
Let's write out what these actually mean.
2 cubed is three 2s multiplied together, and 2 squared is two more 2s.
Line them all up.
Now count what you have. One long line of 2s multiplied, 3 of them, then 2 more.
That is 5 twos in all.
So 2 cubed times 2 squared equals 2⁵.
Always check. 2⁵ equals 32, and 8 times 4 equals 32 as well.
It matches, so the rule held.
And it works for any base at all. 5⁴ times 5 cubed equals 5⁴⁺³ equals 5⁷.
Here is the trap almost everybody falls into.

text: Don't multiply the exponents, and don't multiply the bases.
2 cubed times 2 squared is 2⁵, not 2⁶ and not 4⁵.
Your first thought might be to divide the exponents, 5 divided by 3.
But that is not even a whole number, so it cannot be right.
You could work out 32 divided by 8 instead, and that is fine here. It is no help at all for something like 2²⁰ divided by 2¹⁷.
When you divide powers with the same base, keep the base and subtract the exponents, top minus bottom.
Let's write the division as a fraction.
Five 2s multiplied on the top, three 2s multiplied on the bottom.
Now pair them off. Each 2 on the bottom cancels one 2 on the top, because 2 divided by 2 equals 1.
Three pairs cancel, and two 2s are left up top.
That is 5 minus 3 equals 2, so 2⁵ divided by 2 cubed equals 2 squared.
Check it. 2 squared equals 4, and 32 divided by 8 equals 4 too.
It matches, so the tournament has 4 teams.
And it works for any base you like. 7⁶ divided by 7 squared equals 7⁶⁻² equals 7⁴.
Here is the one to watch for.

text: Don't divide the exponents — subtract them.
2⁶ divided by 2 cubed is 2⁶⁻³ equals 2 cubed, not 2 squared.
You see a 3 and a 2 sitting there, and adding them is tempting. That would give 2⁵.
But look at what the outside 2 is really asking for, 2 cubed times 2 cubed.
And that is not five 2s.
When you raise a power to another exponent, keep the base and multiply the exponents.
The outside exponent is a 2, and it is counting copies.
It says, write 2 cubed down two times and multiply them.
So (2 cubed)² equals 2 cubed times 2 cubed.
Now count every 2. Each copy has three of them, and there are 2 copies.
Copies of the same power means you multiply the exponents.
So (2 cubed)² equals 2⁶.
Try a bigger one. (5⁴)³ is three copies of 5⁴.
That is 4 plus 4 plus 4 equals 12 fives, which is just 4 times 3.
So (5⁴)³ equals 5¹².
This is the one that catches people.
Don't add the exponents here.
The outside exponent counts copies, so you multiply, (2 cubed)² is 2⁶, not 2⁵.
Try to read 2⁰ the old way and it falls apart. Zero 2s multiplied together?
And 2⁻¹ would be minus one 2, which is not a thing anybody can count.
Counting is not going to help us here. We need another way to look at it.
Each time the exponent goes down by 1, divide by the base.
So 2⁰ equals 1, and 2⁻¹ equals one half.
Read along the row with me, left to right.
Every time the exponent drops by 1, the value gets divided by 2.
Look, 8 divided by 2 equals 4, and 4 divided by 2 equals 2.
Now just keep the pattern going. One step past 2¹ equals 2, divide by 2 again.
2 divided by 2 equals 1, so 2⁰ equals 1.
One more step down. 1 divided by 2 equals one half, so 2⁻¹ equals one half. Another step, and 2⁻² equals one fourth.
So a negative exponent means 1 over the positive one.
That is 2⁻² equals one half squared equals one fourth.
Here is the trap. A negative exponent does not make a negative answer.
2⁻² is one fourth, a small positive number.
It is not negative 4.
The trouble with all those zeros is that one slip changes everything. Drop a single zero and the number is 10 times too small.
Quick, which is bigger, 150,000,000 or 15,000,000?
You had to count them, and so does everybody else.
Write a big number as a number from 1 up to 10, times a power of 10.
The exponent counts how many places the point moved.
First job, get a number between 1 and 10. Put the point right after the first digit.
And 1.5 sits neatly between 1 and 10.
Now count how far the point has to jump to get back. From 1.5 to 150,000,000 is 8 places to the right.
Every jump is one times 10, so 8 jumps is times 10⁸.
That gives us 150,000,000 equals 1.5 times 10⁸.
Let's do one more, a smaller one.
4,200 equals 4.2 times 10 cubed, because the point jumps 3 places to make 4.2.
One warning before you go.
Don't just count the digits and use that.
150,000,000 has 9 digits, but the point only moves 8 places.
You might reach for 5.2 times 10⁴. But that is 52,000, which is enormous.
Our grain of pollen is less than 1.
So a positive exponent is never going to work here.
For a small number, the point moves right to make a number from 1 up to 10.
The exponent is negative and counts the places.
Move the point to the right, and keep going until it sits just after the first digit that is not a zero.
So 0.00052 becomes 5.2.
Count the jumps that took, 4 of them.
Now go back the other way. From 5.2 to 0.00052 you divide by 10 four times.
And you already know 10⁻¹ equals one tenth, so dividing by 10 four times is the same as times 10⁻⁴.
That means 0.00052 equals 5.2 times 10⁻⁴.
Here is a shorter one.
0.03 equals 3 times 10⁻², because the point jumps 2 places to the right to make 3.
Watch this one carefully.
Don't count only the zeros after the point.
0.00052 has 3 of them, but the point jumps 4 places to land past the 5.
You could write these out the long way, 30,000 times 2,000, and count the zeros.
That is fine for small ones.
But a number like 3 times 10²¹ would need 21 zeros written out first, and nobody wants that.
Multiply the front numbers, and add the exponents of 10.
If the front number is 10 or more, move its point one place and add 1 to the exponent.
When you multiply, the order does not matter at all.
So slide the front numbers together, and the powers of 10 together.
Then 3 times 2 equals 6.
Now the powers of 10. Same base, so add the exponents.
That is 10⁷.
So the warehouse holds 6 times 10⁷ screws.
Now try this one, (4 times 10⁵) times (5 times 10 squared). 4 times 5 equals 20, and 10⁵ times 10 squared equals 10⁷.
But hold on. 20 is not under 10, so we are not finished.
20 is itself 2 times 10¹, and that extra 10 joins the others, so the answer is 2 times 10⁸.
One last thing.
Don't leave a front number of 10 or more.
20 times 10⁷ has exactly the right value, but the short way needs 2 times 10⁸.
Dividing feels like the obvious move, so let's try it. Half of 25 is 12.5.
And a third of 27 is 9. Neither of those is the side.
What we are hunting for is a number that multiplies with itself.
To undo squaring, find the number that times itself makes it.
To undo cubing, find the number that, used three times, makes it.
Start with the patio. It is a square, so side times side has to make 25.
Well, 5 times 5 equals 25, so the side is 5 tiles.
There is a symbol for that hunt, and we write it the square root of 25 equals 5.
Now the box. It is a cube, so side times side times side has to make 27.
And 3 times 3 times 3 equals 27, so the side is 3 cubes.

Then you read the table backwards. 16 sits in the 4 column, so the square root of 16 equals 4.
And 64 is in that same column, so ∛64 equals 4.

Don't divide by 2 to find a square root.
the square root of 36 is 6, not 18, because 6 times 6 equals 36. And ∛27 is not 27 divided by 3 either.
Try the whole numbers first. 4 times 4 equals 16, and that is too small.
5 times 5 equals 25, and that is too big.
No whole number times itself makes 20, so we are going to have to close in on it.
Find the perfect squares just below and just above the number.
The square root is between their roots, nearer the closer square.
So find the perfect squares on each side of 20. They are 16 and 25.
That means the square root of 20 has to sit between the square root of 16 equals 4 and the square root of 25 equals 5.
Now measure the two gaps. 20 is 4 away from 16, but 5 away from 25.
So 20 leans toward 16, which means the square root of 20 leans toward 4.
Let's test that. Halfway between 4 and 5 is 4.5.
And 4.5 times 4.5 equals 20.25, which is a little more than 20.
So the square root of 20 is just under 4.5, which puts it nearer to 4.

Don't halve the number.

So how steep is it?
You could say quite steep — but that does not help anyone actually build a ramp.
And look, the line keeps going forever, so you cannot just measure how tall it is.
Go across from one point, then up to the next.
Divide how far up (the rise) by how far across (the run).

Now walk right along the bottom until you are straight under (3, 4).
You went 2 across. That is the run.
Now climb straight up to (3, 4).
You went 3 up. That is the rise.

Now divide, with the rise on top.

Here is the one that catches people.

You could work out each walker on their own, minute by minute.

A function gives exactly one output for each input.

Keep going and every input shows up exactly once, with one output each.

Now watch this one.
Input 2 shows up twice. Once it gives 6, and once it gives 8.

Our input is 4.

So an input of 4 gives an output of 10.
Do that same work for other inputs and you can fill a whole table.

In 3 times 4 minus 2 you multiply 3 times 4 first, and then take the 2 away.
Look at both tables.
Plant A gets taller every week, and so does Plant B.

These two do not even look alike. One is a table and one is a rule.

That plus 2 in Ben's rule is where he starts, not how fast he grows.

The amount paid once is added on.

Now the part that repeats. Each month adds another 10 dollars, so x months add 10 times x.

Going down does not mean Sam is riding downhill. It means he is getting closer to home.

This time the y stays put, and it is the x that changes sign.

A stretch multiplies, and it multiplies both coordinates.
Maybe the sides just grew by the same amount. Let's test that.
The bottom went from 4 to 8, so that is 4 more. But the side of 3 went to 6, and that is only 3 more.
Different amounts. So adding is not what is going on here.
Triangles with the same angles have sides that all grow by the same scale factor.
Find it from one matching pair, then multiply.
Look at the corners for a moment, not the sides.
Every corner of the big sign has exactly the same angle as a corner of the small one.
That is what tells you which side goes with which. Each side of the big sign matches the side sitting in the same place on the small one.
Now pick one pair where you know both sides. The bottoms, 4 grew to 8, and 8 divided by 4 equals 2.
Always check that on a second pair before you trust it.
3 times 2 equals 6, and 6 is exactly what the big sign says. So every side is 2 times as long.
Back to the side we came for. The missing one matches the 2 foot side on the small sign.
So multiply it by the scale factor, 2 times 2 equals 4.
The missing side is 4 feet, and now every side of the big sign is filled in.
Here is the trap, and it is the one from the beginning.
Don't add the difference you saw between two sides.
Similar triangles grow by multiplying, so multiply by the scale factor every time.
Now, you cannot just go and measure that one.
The top corner is way up on the roof, and nobody is holding a protractor up there.
So we need a rule that finds the angle without measuring it at all.
The three angles inside a triangle always add to 180 degrees.
The angle outside one corner equals the two far inside angles added.
Here is something you can try with paper.
Tear the three corners off a paper triangle, then push their points together.
They line up. Every time, they make one straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees.
So back to the roof. Add up the two angles you were given.
50 plus 60 equals 110, and the third one is whatever is left over out of 180.
180 minus 110 equals 70. The top angle is 70 degrees.
Now stretch the bottom side out past the 60 degrees corner.
The angle that opens up outside is 180 minus 60 equals 120 degrees.
Here is the neat part. That is exactly the two far angles added together, 50 plus 70 equals 120.
This is the one that catches people out.
Don't stop after adding the two angles you know.
That total is not the answer. Take it away from 180 degrees first.
Your first thought might be to add, 4 plus 3 equals 7.
But look at what 7 really is. That is the long way, around the corner.
The straight path has to be shorter than 7, so adding is not the rule we want.
In a right triangle, square the two short sides and add them.
That makes the square of the long side.
Watch this. Draw a square out from each side of the triangle.
The square sitting on the 3 side holds 3 times 3 equals 9 little squares.
The one on the 4 side holds 4 times 4 equals 16.
Now tip those two squares into the big one on the long side.
9 plus 16 equals 25.
The big square holds exactly 25 little squares. Not one over, not one short.
So the long side, squared, is 25. Now work backward. Which number times itself makes 25?
5 times 5 equals 25.
So the path straight across the park is 5 blocks.
One last time, because this is the whole point.
Don't add the sides themselves.
Add their squares, and then find the number that times itself gives you that total.
Careful here, because something has changed.
Last time you added the squares to find the long side. This time the ladder is the long side, and it is the one you already know.
If you added, you would get a height longer than the ladder itself, and that cannot happen.
When you know the long side, square it and take away the square of the short side you know.
Then undo the square.
Build the squares again, the same way you did before.
The square on the 5 meter ladder holds 5 times 5 equals 25. The square on the 3 meter side holds 3 times 3 equals 9.
And the third one is the square we are hunting for.
Remember the rule, the two small squares together fill the big one exactly.
So the missing square is whatever is left when you take 9 out of 25.
25 minus 9 equals 16.
Now undo the square, just like last lesson.
Which number times itself makes 16? 4 times 4 equals 16.
So the ladder reaches 4 meters up the wall.
Here is the mix-up between these last two lessons.
Don't add when the long side is already the one you know.
Its square is the total, so this time you take away.
Draw the straight path in and look at it closely.
It cuts across the squares on a slant, right through their middles.
So counting squares along that line will not tell you how long it is.
Draw a right triangle between the two points.
Count its legs on the grid, then find the hypotenuse.
Start at (1, 1) and go straight across, then turn and go straight up to (4, 5).
Now look at that corner where the two paths meet.
It is a square corner, so what you have drawn is a right triangle.
Now measure the two legs. You can do that with subtraction instead of counting.
Across, 4 minus 1 equals 3. Up, 5 minus 1 equals 4.
So the legs are 3 miles and 4 miles.
Now it is the same job as last lesson.
Square the legs and add, 3 times 3 plus 4 times 4 equals 9 plus 16 equals 25.
Then undo the square. 5 times 5 equals 25, so the two towns are 5 miles apart.
And the trap is the same one as before.
Don't add the legs.
3 plus 4 equals 7 is the walk along the grid lines, around the corner, not the straight line across.
In a box you could stack little cubes and just count them up.
A can is round, though.
Line cubes up against that curved side and you get gaps everywhere.
A cylinder is a stack of circles.
Find the area of the circle, 3.14 times radius times radius, then multiply by the height.
Start at the circle on the bottom.
From the center out to the edge is 2 in, so that is the radius.
The area of a circle is 3.14 times the radius times the radius.
That gives us 12.56 square inches in one layer.
Now stack that circle up the can.
Every inch of height is one more layer of 12.56.
The can is 5 in tall, so we get 5 layers.
One layer is 12.56, and we want 5 of them.
12.56 times 5 equals 62.8.
Written out in one go, that is 3.14 times 2 times 2 times 5, the circle and then the height.
So your can holds 62.8 cubic inches of soup.
Don't use the distance all the way across.
This can is 4 in across, but the rule wants the radius, and that is 2 in.
Watch what happens as you go up this cup.
A cone is not the same all the way up.
Its circles get smaller and smaller until they shrink to a point, so there is no one circle to stack again and again.
A cone holds one third of the cylinder with the same bottom and height.
Find the cylinder, then divide by 3.
Try this one for real.
Fill the cone with water, then pour it into a cylinder with the same bottom and the same height.
One pour, and the cylinder is only a third full.
It takes 3 whole cones to fill it.
So forget the cone for a moment.
Build the cylinder with that same bottom and that same height.
Circle times height, 3.14 times 3 times 3 times 4 equals 113.04 cubic centimeters.
Now bring the cone back.
It holds one third of what that cylinder holds.
So we divide, 113.04 divided by 3 equals 37.68.
Your paper cup holds 37.68 cubic centimeters of water.
Here is where people lose the point.
Don't stop once you have the cylinder.
A cone holds only one third of it, so you have to divide by 3 at the end.
Here is the problem with a ball.
It has no flat bottom to stack layers on, and no straight height to stack them up.
Our cylinder rule has nothing to hold on to.
A ball fills two thirds of the can that fits around it.
Its volume is four thirds times 3.14 times radius times radius times radius.
Picture the smallest can this ball would fit inside, snug.
It has the same radius as the ball, 3 in.
And its height is the whole way across the ball, so 3 times 2 equals 6 in.
Fill that can right to the top with water, then push the ball down into it.
The water that spills over the side is exactly the size of the ball.
Two thirds of the can spills out, and only one third stays in.
The can first, 3.14 times 3 times 3 times 6 equals 169.56.
The ball is two thirds of that, so 169.56 divided by 3 times 2 equals 113.04.
And that is exactly what the rule gives you, with the radius in three times.
The ball holds 113.04 cubic inches.
Don't use the radius only twice, the way you would for a flat circle.
A ball is round in every direction, so the radius goes in three times.
There is no single rule that fits this whole thing.
So look at it in two parts.
The bottom is a cone.
The scoop on top is half of a ball.
First name each shape, can, cone or ball.
Use its rule, and add the pieces when one object is made of two shapes.
Take the cone first.
It is one third of the cylinder with that same bottom and that same height.
So we get 37.68 cubic centimeters.
Now the scoop on top.
Find a whole ball first, four thirds times 3.14 times 3 times 3 times 3 equals 113.04.
But only half a ball is sitting up there, so cut that in half.
113.04 divided by 2 equals 56.52.
Two pieces, two numbers.
37.68 from the cone, and 56.52 from the scoop.
Add them, 37.68 plus 56.52 equals 94.2.
That is 94.2 cubic centimeters of ice cream in all.
One last thing to watch for.
Don't add a whole ball when only half of one is sitting on top.
Halve it first, then add.

Put one question in the rows and one in the columns.

Counts from groups of different sizes do not compare fairly.
